data.title: Remote Repository
data.tagline: A repository accessible elsewhere that exchanges commits with a local repository
data.description: You commit B locally, while remote main (origin) on GitHub still points to A; B exists only on your computer until push sends it to the remote. A teammate can then build commit C on the remote history. If the remote has commits missing locally, a direct push is rejected. Pull fetches first, then integrates remote commits using the configured merge or rebase behavior. origin is a common remote name; pushing to a repository does not mean a website has been deployed.

use: After a rejected push, review remote commits, pull to integrate them, then decide whether to push
Clone copies the remote’s current commits and commonly names that remote origin
avoid: Commit secrets or .env files and push them
Force push over remote history after a rejection
Push to the wrong remote address
Assume pushing means the site is deployed
scenarios: Local commit B has not been sent to the remote
Both sides have A and B after push
A teammate adds C and local push is rejected
Pull integrates C according to configuration

lessonPractice.title: Local has A and B, while the remote also has a teammate’s C; push is rejected. What next?

options.label: Review C, then use git pull with the project’s configured integration behavior before deciding whether to push
options.feedback: Correct. Pull fetches first, then integrates using the configured merge/rebase behavior. Keep and review the teammate's C before deciding whether to push.

options.label: Run git push --force to overwrite the remote’s C
options.feedback: A force push can remove C, which the teammate already pushed. Understand and integrate that commit rather than overwriting it to make push succeed.

options.label: Rename local main and push it to the same remote
options.feedback: Renaming the local branch does not integrate C; the remote history is still ahead and the push problem remains.

data.agentPrompt: Run git fetch origin, then compare local main with the updated local remote-tracking reference origin/main. If remote main (origin) has a teammate’s C, explain what it changes, then run git pull using the project’s configured merge/rebase behavior and resolve any conflicts. Confirm C is preserved and the page still works before pushing; explain that push syncs to the remote but does not mean the site was deployed.
